title: Complexity of Unit-Time Precedence Scheduling on Three Machines
short_statement: The classical three-machine, unit-job precedence scheduling question now has a reported polynomial-time exact algorithm awaiting independent verification.
full_statement: An instance consists of a finite set $J$ of unit-processing-time jobs, three identical parallel machines, and a precedence partial order $\prec$ on $J$. A feasible nonpreemptive schedule assigns each job $j\in J$ to one of the three machines and to an integer time slot, with at most one job processed on each machine in each slot, and with $j$ completed before $k$ starts whenever $j\prec k$. The objective is to minimize the makespan $C_{\max}$, the time at which the last job completes. The original problem asks for the classical decision complexity of this clean fixed-machine model: given $T$, decide whether there is a feasible schedule of makespan at most $T$ for $P3\mid prec,p_j=1\mid C_{\max}$. A September 2026 manuscript claims a polynomial-time exact solution of this model. The claim has not been independently certified in this audit.
background: Precedence-constrained scheduling is a classical meeting point of operations research and algorithms. Jobs are all unit length and only their partial order creates difficulty. Two machines admit special polynomial structure; allowing the machine count to vary changes the complexity. For decades, the exact complexity with three machines remained a prominent question from Garey and Johnson's list. Quasi-polynomial approximation schemes improved the optimization picture without settling that exact question. A September 2026 manuscript now claims a polynomial-time exact algorithm for the original three-machine model. The reported bound is enormous, and the proof requires independent scrutiny; the historical question is therefore recorded as solution claimed rather than plainly open.
known_results:
Earlier hierarchy-based and combinatorial approximation schemes approximate fixed-machine precedence scheduling in quasi-polynomial time but do not decide exact feasibility.

OpenAI, 'A Polynomial-Time Algorithm for Three-Machine Unit-Job Scheduling' (September 24, 2026), Theorem 1.1, claims a uniform deterministic algorithm producing an optimal schedule and deciding deadlines in $O((L+2)^{150020})$ Turing-machine steps, where $L$ is the complete binary input length. The input is an arbitrary explicitly listed precedence DAG, with three identical machines and unit, nonpreemptive jobs; there are no release dates or communication delays. The claimed exponent is constant but impractical.

This is a claimed full resolution of the original complexity target, not merely an approximation result. This audit checked the theorem and model, but did not independently certify the complete proof or a formalization.
open_problem: Claimed resolution: the three-machine unit-job precedence scheduling problem is in P. Independently verify the reported algorithm and proof; this entry no longer presents the original complexity question as plainly open. Practical running time and extensions are separate questions.

counterexample_rationale: A hardness proof would likely require a finite gadget construction, and automated search might help discover small precedence gadgets. A polynomial-time resolution would probably require structural decomposition rather than a finite counterexample.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search over small posets, minimal unschedulable instances, and candidate reductions could expose useful gadgets or invariants. However, a final answer needs a formal complexity proof.

literature.synthesis: Approximation schemes and exact complexity must be separated. The new manuscript addresses the original decision and optimization problems directly. Its correctness needs independent assessment; faster useful algorithms would be a follow-up target, not a reason to continue calling the original question open.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Prioritize verification of the reported decomposition and dynamic program. Small-poset enumeration can test structural lemmas and schedule reconstruction, but cannot certify correctness for every input. Improving the enormous polynomial exponent or extending the model would be follow-up results, not a new resolution of the original decision question.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: Referee the bounded-description decomposition and its closure under recursion, completeness of the dynamic program, exact schedule reconstruction, and uniform bit complexity. Do not infer a practical algorithm or a result for release dates, arbitrary processing lengths, or communication delays. No formal certificate was replayed by this audit.
